Reads coordinates in any of the usual formats

Source: R/coordinates.R
parse_coordinates.Rd

Meant for copying and pasting the position of a point from Google Earth, Google Maps or a GPS. Recognises:

Usage

parse_coordinates(text)

Arguments

text

Text with the coordinates, or a numeric vector c(latitude, longitude) (named c(lat = , lon = ) in any order).

Value

A list with lat, lon (decimal degrees, WGS84) and precision_m: approximate uncertainty (metres) due to the number of decimals written.

Details

FormatExample
Decimal degrees (Google Maps / Earth)"41.123456, -3.123456"
Degrees, minutes and seconds"41°07'24.4\"N 3°07'24.4\"W"
Spanish hemisphere letters (O = west)"41°07'24.4\"N 3°07'24.4\"O"
Degrees and decimal minutes"41°07.407'N 3°07.407'W"
Hemisphere first (handheld GPS)"N41 07.407 W3 07.407"
Hemisphere words"41.1234 North, 3.1234 West"
Without symbols"41 07 24.4 N 3 07 24.4 W"
Google Earth placemark (KML)"<coordinates>-3.1234,41.1234,0</coordinates>"
Google Maps link (marked point)"https://www.google.com/maps?q=41.1234,-3.1234"
Decimal comma"41,123456 -3,123456"
Numeric vectorc(41.123456, -3.123456) or c(lon = -3.1, lat = 41.1)

Without hemisphere letters the latitude goes first (as in Google) and a negative longitude is west. Typographic minus signs and quotes (copied from PDF or Word documents) are accepted. Texts that do not contain coordinates (short links, Plus Codes, notes) are rejected.

Examples

parse_coordinates("41.123456, -3.123456")
#> $lat
#> [1] 41.12346
#> 
#> $lon
#> [1] -3.123456
#> 
#> $precision_m
#> [1] 1
#> 
parse_coordinates("41°07'24.4\"N 3°07'24.4\"O")
#> $lat
#> [1] 41.12344
#> 
#> $lon
#> [1] -3.123444
#> 
#> $precision_m
#> [1] 2
#> 
parse_coordinates("N41 07.407 W3 07.407")
#> $lat
#> [1] 41.12345
#> 
#> $lon
#> [1] -3.12345
#> 
#> $precision_m
#> [1] 2
#> 
parse_coordinates(c(41.12, -3.12))
#> $lat
#> [1] 41.12
#> 
#> $lon
#> [1] -3.12
#> 
#> $precision_m
#> [1] 697
#>
